title: PPFD Mapping, Uniformity and Canopy Measurement

content.overview: PPFD is most useful when measured across the actual canopy. A grid of repeated measurements reveals intensity gradients and uniformity that a single center reading cannot show.

vocabulary.definition: Photosynthetic photon flux density, the photon flux in the photosynthetically active waveband reaching a surface.
The degree to which measured light intensity is distributed consistently across a defined canopy area.
A repeatable set of canopy positions used to compare light distribution spatially.

sections.title: One reading is not a canopy map
sections.body: Fixture geometry, hanging height, reflectance, plant spacing, and canopy shape create spatial differences. Multiple points are needed to characterize the distribution growers actually manage.

sections.title: Measure at the crop plane
sections.body: Measurements should be made at a defined height and orientation that represents the crop surface. Changing sensor angle or elevation can make repeated maps difficult to compare.

sections.title: Uniformity can matter as much as average intensity
sections.body: An acceptable average can conceal excessively bright and dim regions. Uniformity analysis helps determine whether fixture layout or canopy arrangement should change.

workedExamples: A nine-point grid averaging 700 can still contain a center at 1000 and corners at 450; the average alone hides the distribution problem.
After changing fixture height, repeat the same grid to determine whether uniformity improved rather than judging visually.
A 4×4 map averages 720 µmol/m²/s but ranges from 430 to 980. The mean is acceptable only if the distribution is also evaluated.
After lowering fixtures, average PPFD rises 12% but corner values barely change. The change improved intensity more than uniformity.
commonMistakes: Using only the brightest center point.
Comparing meters without confirming their calibration or measurement method.
Failing to record fixture output setting or canopy height with the map.
content.practicalApplication: Define a canopy grid, measure PPFD at consistent height and orientation, calculate the average and range, map hot and dim zones, and repeat after major fixture or canopy changes.
content.summary: PPFD mapping turns lighting from a fixture specification into a crop-level measurement. Repeatable spatial data reveal intensity and uniformity across the canopy.

blocks.title: PPFD mapping is spatial measurement
blocks.body: A canopy is not exposed to one number. Mapping converts many point measurements into a spatial picture that can reveal hotspots, edge losses and changes caused by fixture height or canopy architecture.

rows: Links light map to plant geometry

items.body: Use repeatable coordinates across the crop area.

items.title: Calculate summary values
items.body: Use average, min, max and distribution pattern.

items.title: Compare with crop layout
items.body: Identify whether fixture or canopy geometry explains the pattern.

blocks.setting: The map average is 700, but several corners are below 450 while the center exceeds 950.
options: The average plus spatial nonuniformity and hotspot/dim zones
blocks.answer: The average plus spatial nonuniformity and hotspot/dim zones.
blocks.feedback: The average alone hides the crop-relevant distribution.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.body: A repeatable grid is more informative than one impressive center reading.
